catalog_description: Effective sensing area of flux loop coil.
catalog_documentation:
Effective sensing area $A_{\text{eff}}$ of a flux loop diagnostic coil, defined as the product of the number of turns and the area enclosed by each turn. The effective area converts measured voltage to magnetic flux change via integration and is critical for quantitative magnetic measurements and equilibrium reconstruction.

$$A_{\text{eff}} = N \times A_{\text{turn}}$$

where $N$ is the number of turns (dimensionless), $A_{\text{turn}}$ is the area per turn in m$^2$, giving $A_{\text{eff}}$ in m$^2$.

Physical significance:

The effective area converts measured voltage to magnetic flux change via integration. Accurate calibration of flux loop effective area is critical for quantitative magnetic measurements and equilibrium reconstruction. Area affects [flux_loop_voltage](#flux_loop_voltage) calibration and determines measurement sensitivity. See [flux_loop_voltage](#flux_loop_voltage) for measurement relationships and [magnetic_flux](#magnetic_flux) for flux calculations.

Measurement relation:

The effective area converts measured voltage to magnetic flux change via integration:

$$\Delta \Psi = \frac{1}{A_{\text{eff}}} \int V \, dt$$

where $V$ is [flux_loop_voltage](#flux_loop_voltage) in V, $t$ is time in s, and $\Delta \Psi$ is flux change in Wb.

Measurement methods:

Flux loop area is determined from coil geometry measurements including turn count and loop dimensions. Calibration procedures use known magnetic fields for area verification. Area calibration affects [flux_loop_voltage](#flux_loop_voltage) interpretation and equilibrium reconstruction accuracy. Engineering survey techniques measure coil positioning and geometry. Area stability is monitored over time.

Typical values:

0.01-1 m$^2$ depending on coil design and installation location. Area typically ranges from small diagnostic loops to large vessel-encompassing coils.

Sign convention: Positive area follows the right-hand rule for loop orientation, consistent with [flux_loop_voltage](#flux_loop_voltage) measurements and magnetic flux conventions.

Electron number density $n_e$ representing the volumetric concentration of electrons (thermal plus non-thermal) in the plasma. In fusion plasmas, electron density typically ranges from $10^{18}$ m$^{-3}$ in the edge region to $10^{20}$ m$^{-3}$ in the plasma core. Electron density determines plasma conductivity and affects [plasma_resistivity](#plasma_resistivity).

Thermodynamic relation:

Electron density relates to [electron_pressure](#electron_pressure) and [electron_temperature](#electron_temperature) via the ideal gas law:

$$p_e = n_e k_B T_e$$

where $p_e$ is electron pressure in Pa, $k_B = 1.381 \times 10^{-23}$ J/K is Boltzmann's constant, and $T_e$ is in K. When using $T_e$ in eV, apply conversion: $p_e = n_e T_e \times 1.602 \times 10^{-19}$ Pa.

Physical significance:

Electron density determines plasma conductivity through $\sigma = n_e e^2 \tau / m_e$ and affects [plasma_current](#plasma_current) requirements. Higher density improves confinement through increased collisionality but may reduce [energy_confinement_time](#energy_confinement_time). Density gradients drive [electron_heat_flux](#electron_heat_flux) and affect [plasma_current_density](#plasma_current_density) profiles. See [plasma_density_at_magnetic_axis](#plasma_density_at_magnetic_axis) for core values.

Measurement methods:

Interferometry measures line-integrated electron density through phase shift of laser beams. Reflectometry determines density profiles from microwave reflection. Thomson scattering provides local density measurements with high spatial resolution. Interferometry systems use multiple chords for 2D reconstruction. Density measurements are essential for [electron_pressure](#electron_pressure) calculations and equilibrium reconstruction.

Typical values:

Edge region: $10^{18}$-$10^{19}$ m$^{-3}$, core region: $10^{19}$-$10^{20}$ m$^{-3}$ in high-performance tokamak plasmas. On-axis values in [plasma_density_at_magnetic_axis](#plasma_density_at_magnetic_axis) typically reach $5 \times 10^{19}$ - $2 \times 10^{20}$ m$^{-3}$ during high-performance operation.

Sign convention: Positive density indicates particle concentration, following standard plasma physics conventions.

Electron kinetic temperature $T_e$ representing the mean thermal energy per electron. In fusion plasmas, electron temperature typically ranges from tens of eV in the edge region to several keV in the plasma core.

Thermodynamic relation:

Electron temperature relates to [electron_pressure](#electron_pressure) via the ideal gas law:

$$p_e = n_e k_B T_e$$

where $n_e$ is [electron_density](#electron_density) in m$^{-3}$, $k_B = 1.381 \times 10^{-23}$ J/K is Boltzmann's constant, $T_e$ is in K, giving $p_e$ in Pa. When using $T_e$ in eV, apply conversion: $p_e = n_e T_e \times 1.602 \times 10^{-19}$ Pa.

Physical significance:

Temperature determines [energy_confinement_time](#energy_confinement_time) and fusion reactivity. Higher electron temperatures improve confinement quality and increase fusion reaction rates. The temperature gradient drives [electron_heat_flux](#electron_heat_flux) and affects [plasma_resistivity](#plasma_resistivity). See also [ion_temperature](#ion_temperature) and [electron_temperature_at_magnetic_axis](#electron_temperature_at_magnetic_axis).

Measurement methods:

Thomson scattering provides local [electron_density](#electron_density) and temperature measurements. Electron cyclotron emission measures temperature from radiation spectrum. X-ray spectroscopy determines temperature from continuum and line emissions. Interferometry provides line-integrated density for pressure calculations.

Typical values:

Edge region: 10-200 eV, core region: 1-20 keV in high-performance tokamak plasmas. On-axis values in [electron_temperature_at_magnetic_axis](#electron_temperature_at_magnetic_axis) typically reach 5-15 keV during auxiliary heating.

Electron temperature $T_{e,0}$ evaluated at the [magnetic_axis](#magnetic_axis), representing the peak electron temperature in the plasma core. The magnetic axis is the innermost flux surface where the poloidal magnetic field vanishes and plasma parameters typically reach maximum values. On-axis electron temperature is a key indicator of core plasma performance and confinement quality.

Performance significance:

On-axis electron temperature is used in metrics such as the fusion triple product $n T \tau_E$ where $n$ is density in m$^{-3}$, $T$ is temperature in keV, and $\tau_E$ is [energy_confinement_time](#energy_confinement_time) in s. Higher on-axis temperature improves fusion reactivity and determines [plasma_current](#plasma_current) requirements. Temperature affects [plasma_resistivity](#plasma_resistivity) and [heating_power_due_to_ohmic](#heating_power_due_to_ohmic) efficiency. See [electron_temperature](#electron_temperature) for profile context and [ion_temperature_at_magnetic_axis](#ion_temperature_at_magnetic_axis) for ion temperatures.

Measurement methods:

Electron temperature at magnetic axis is measured using Thomson scattering systems focused on the plasma center. Electron cyclotron emission radiometry provides continuous temperature monitoring at the axis. X-ray crystal spectroscopy measures temperature from continuum radiation. MSE (motional Stark effect) diagnostics can provide temperature measurements in some configurations. On-axis measurements require precise alignment with [magnetic_axis](#magnetic_axis) location.

Typical values:

High-performance H-mode: 5-20 keV, ohmic plasmas: 1-5 keV. On-axis temperature typically exceeds edge values by factor of 2-5 depending on heating power and confinement regime.

Sign convention: Positive temperature indicates thermal energy per electron, following standard thermodynamic conventions with temperature measured in energy units (eV or keV).

Plasma cross-section elongation evaluated specifically at the [plasma_boundary](#plasma_boundary) (last closed flux surface). Boundary elongation is a key shape parameter for tokamak design and operation, affecting [plasma_volume](#plasma_volume) and [energy_confinement_time](#energy_confinement_time) through geometric effects.

$$\kappa_{\text{boundary}} = \frac{b}{a}$$

where $b$ is half-height of plasma boundary and $a$ is [minor_radius_of_plasma_boundary](#minor_radius_of_plasma_boundary).

Physical significance:

Boundary elongation is a key shape parameter for tokamak design and operation. Higher elongation increases [plasma_volume](#plasma_volume) and improves confinement through favorable geometric effects, but also increases susceptibility to [vertical_displacement_event](#vertical_displacement_event) requiring active feedback control. Elongation affects [plasma_current](#plasma_current) limits and [safety_factor](#safety_factor) requirements. See [radial_coordinate_of_plasma_boundary](#radial_coordinate_of_plasma_boundary) and [minor_radius_of_plasma_boundary](#minor_radius_of_plasma_boundary) for geometric relationships.

Relation to plasma current:

For fixed aspect ratio and [safety_factor](#safety_factor), higher elongation allows higher [plasma_current](#plasma_current): $I_p \propto \kappa$. This relationship is fundamental for tokamak scaling and operational limits.

Measurement methods:

Elongation is determined from equilibrium reconstruction using external [magnetic_field](#magnetic_field) measurements. [Flux_loop_voltage](#flux_loop_voltage) integration provides boundary shape information. Plasma imaging systems measure boundary geometry directly. Shape analysis requires [magnetic_axis](#magnetic_axis) location and [plasma_boundary](#plasma_boundary) identification. Elongation is calculated from boundary coordinates in the poloidal plane.

Typical values:

Circular plasmas: $\kappa \approx 1.0$, moderately shaped: $\kappa = 1.5$-1.8, highly elongated: $\kappa = 2.0$-2.5. Elongation is actively controlled through external coil currents.

Sign convention: Positive when $\kappa \geq 1$ indicating vertically elongated or circular cross-section, following standard tokamak geometry conventions.

Energy confinement time $\tau_E$ quantifying how long thermal energy is retained in the plasma before being lost to the surroundings. This is the single most important figure of merit for fusion performance and determines the approach to ignition conditions.

$$\tau_E = \frac{W_{\text{th}}}{P_{\text{loss}}}$$

where $W_{\text{th}}$ is total thermal energy content in J and $P_{\text{loss}}$ is total power loss in W.

Physical significance:

Energy confinement time determines fusion performance through the triple product $n T \tau_E$. Longer confinement times enable higher plasma temperatures and pressures, approaching fusion ignition conditions. The fusion triple product criterion requires $n T \tau_E > 3 \times 10^{21}$ m$^{-3}$ keV s for D-T fusion. Confinement quality affects [plasma_current](#plasma_current) requirements and [safety_factor](#safety_factor) limits for stable operation.

Scaling laws:

Empirical scaling laws predict $\tau_E$ from machine and plasma parameters. H-mode confinement shows $\tau_E \propto I_p^{0.93} B_T^{0.15} P^{-0.69} n^{0.41} R^{1.97} a^{0.58} \kappa^{0.78}$ (IPB98(y,2) scaling), where $I_p$ is [plasma_current](#plasma_current), $B_T$ is toroidal field, $P$ is heating power, and geometric factors follow. Confinement improves with higher current, density, and larger machine size.

Measurement methods:

Energy confinement time is derived from total thermal energy content and power loss measurements. Thermal energy is calculated from [electron_temperature](#electron_temperature) and [ion_temperature](#ion_temperature) profiles integrated over [plasma_volume](#plasma_volume). Power loss includes radiated power, conducted power to walls, and convective losses. [Electron_heat_flux](#electron_heat_flux) measurements provide local transport analysis.

Typical values:

L-mode: 20-50 ms, H-mode: 100-300 ms for medium tokamaks; ITER target: ~4 s. Confinement time scales with machine size and plasma current, following empirical scaling laws.

Minor radius evaluated at the [plasma_boundary](#plasma_boundary) (last closed flux surface), calculated as half the difference between outboard and inboard major radii at the midplane. Minor radius defines the characteristic size scale for normalized radial coordinates and plasma cross-sectional area.

$$a_{\text{boundary}} = \frac{R_{\text{out}} - R_{\text{in}}}{2}$$

where $R_{\text{out}}$ is [radial_coordinate_of_plasma_boundary](#radial_coordinate_of_plasma_boundary) at outboard midplane and $R_{\text{in}}$ is the radial coordinate at the inboard midplane, both in m.

Physical significance:

This quantity defines the radial extent of confined plasma and is used in calculating plasma cross-sectional area, [plasma_volume](#plasma_volume), and shape parameters. It serves as the characteristic length scale for normalized radial coordinates. Minor radius affects [energy_confinement_time](#energy_confinement_time) through scaling laws and determines [plasma_current](#plasma_current) requirements. See [radial_coordinate_of_plasma_boundary](#radial_coordinate_of_plasma_boundary) for aspect ratio and [elongation_of_plasma_boundary](#elongation_of_plasma_boundary) for shape relationships.

Relation to shape parameters:

Together with [elongation_of_plasma_boundary](#elongation_of_plasma_boundary) $\kappa$, determines the plasma cross-sectional area: $A_p \approx \pi a^2 \kappa$. This relationship is fundamental for plasma volume and surface area calculations.

Measurement methods:

Minor radius is determined from equilibrium reconstruction using external [magnetic_field](#magnetic_field) measurements. [Flux_loop_voltage](#flux_loop_voltage) integration provides boundary geometry information. Plasma imaging systems measure boundary coordinates directly. Minor radius analysis requires [magnetic_axis](#magnetic_axis) location and [plasma_boundary](#plasma_boundary) identification. Geometric calculations use standard tokamak coordinate systems.

Typical values:

Small tokamaks: 0.2-0.5 m, medium tokamaks: 0.5-1.0 m, ITER: ~2 m. Minor radius scales with machine size and determines plasma cross-sectional area.

Sign convention: Positive minor radius measured from magnetic axis to boundary, following standard tokamak geometry conventions.

Poloidal magnetic field vector $\mathbf{B}_p$ lying in the poloidal plane (R-Z plane), comprising radial and vertical components. The poloidal field is generated by toroidal [plasma_current](#plasma_current) and external poloidal field coils, providing the rotational transform necessary for tokamak confinement.

$$\mathbf{B}_p = B_R \hat{e}_R + B_Z \hat{e}_Z$$

where $B_R$ is [radial_magnetic_field](#radial_magnetic_field), $B_Z$ is [vertical_magnetic_field](#vertical_magnetic_field), both in T.

Physical significance:

The poloidal field is generated by toroidal [plasma_current](#plasma_current) and external poloidal field coils. It provides the rotational transform of field lines necessary for tokamak confinement and determines plasma shape through equilibrium force balance. Poloidal field strength affects [safety_factor](#safety_factor) profiles and MHD stability limits. See [poloidal_magnetic_field](#poloidal_magnetic_field) for magnitude relationships and [magnetic_field](#magnetic_field) for total field structure.

Relation to plasma current:

The poloidal field relates to [plasma_current_density](#plasma_current_density) via Ampère's law:

$$\nabla \times \mathbf{B}_p = \mu_0 j_{\phi} \hat{e}_{\phi}$$

where $j_{\phi}$ is toroidal current density in A/m$^2$ and $\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}$ H/m.

Measurement methods:

Poloidal magnetic field is measured using magnetic probes and flux loops positioned around the plasma. [Flux_loop_voltage](#flux_loop_voltage) integration provides field change information. Equilibrium reconstruction codes invert external magnetic measurements to determine internal field structure. MSE diagnostics provide direct poloidal field measurements in some devices. Vector field analysis requires multiple measurement locations.

Typical values:

Poloidal field strength typically ranges from 0.1-1 T, much smaller than toroidal field but essential for confinement. Field strength varies with radius and [plasma_current](#plasma_current).

Sign convention: Positive poloidal field follows the right-hand rule for toroidal current direction, consistent with [plasma_current](#plasma_current) measurements and standard tokamak conventions.

It provides the rotational transform of field lines necessary for tokamak confinement and determines plasma shape through equilibrium force balance. Poloidal field strength affects [safety_factor](#safety_factor) profiles and MHD stability limits. See [poloidal_magnetic_field](#poloidal_magnetic_field) for magnitude relationships and [magnetic_field](#magnetic_field) for total field structure.

Relation to plasma current:

The poloidal field relates to [plasma_current_density](#plasma_current_density) via Ampère's law:

$$\nabla \times \mathbf{B}_p = \mu_0 j_{\phi} \hat{e}_{\phi}$$

where $j_{\phi}$ is toroidal current density in A/m$^2$ and $\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}$ H/m.

Measurement methods:

Poloidal magnetic field is measured using magnetic probes and flux loops positioned around the plasma. [Flux_loop_voltage](#flux_loop_voltage) integration provides field change information. Equilibrium reconstruction codes invert external magnetic measurements to determine internal field structure. MSE diagnostics provide direct poloidal field measurements in some devices. Vector field analysis requires multiple measurement locations.

Typical values:

Poloidal field strength typically ranges from 0.1-1 T, much smaller than toroidal field but essential for confinement. Field strength varies with radius and [plasma_current](#plasma_current).

Sign convention: Positive poloidal field follows the right-hand rule for toroidal current direction, consistent with [plasma_current](#plasma_current) measurements and standard tokamak conventions.

catalog_description: Radial component of magnetic field vector.
catalog_documentation:
Radial component of the magnetic field vector $B_R$ in cylindrical coordinates. In axisymmetric tokamak equilibria, the radial component is typically small compared to toroidal and poloidal components but is essential for equilibrium force balance and magnetic flux surface reconstruction.

$$B_R = \mathbf{B} \cdot \hat{e}_R$$

where $\mathbf{B}$ is the total magnetic field in T and $\hat{e}_R$ is the unit vector in the major radius direction.

Physical significance:

In axisymmetric tokamak equilibria, the radial component is typically small compared to toroidal and poloidal components but is essential for equilibrium force balance and magnetic flux surface reconstruction. Radial field affects plasma shaping and stability. Field strength relates to [plasma_current](#plasma_current) distribution and [safety_factor](#safety_factor) profiles. See [magnetic_field](#magnetic_field) for total field structure and [poloidal_magnetic_field](#poloidal_magnetic_field) for vector relationships.

Measurement methods:

Radial magnetic field is measured using magnetic probes positioned at different major radii around the plasma. [Flux_loop_voltage](#flux_loop_voltage) integration provides field change information. Equilibrium reconstruction codes invert external magnetic measurements to determine internal field structure. Radial field analysis requires probes at multiple radial locations. Field measurements are essential for flux surface mapping.

Typical values:

$|B_R|$ ranges from milliTesla to tens of milliTesla, typically 1-2 orders of magnitude smaller than $B_{\phi}$ and $B_Z$. Radial field strength varies with plasma conditions and external coil currents.

Sign convention: Positive outward (increasing R direction), following standard cylindrical coordinate conventions and consistent with tokamak geometry.

Magnetic safety factor $q$ (or $q$-profile) quantifying the pitch of magnetic field lines on a flux surface. The safety factor is fundamental for MHD stability analysis and determines the rational surfaces where instabilities can occur.

$$q = \frac{1}{2\pi} \oint \frac{B_{\phi}}{B_p R} dl_p$$

where $B_{\phi}$ is [toroidal_magnetic_field](#toroidal_magnetic_field), $B_p$ is [poloidal_magnetic_field](#poloidal_magnetic_field), $R$ is major radius, and $dl_p$ is the differential poloidal arc length.

Physical significance:

The safety factor determines MHD stability limits through the Kruskal-Shafranov criterion. Rational surfaces where $q = m/n$ (integer $m$, $n$) are resonant for MHD modes. Lower $q$ values indicate higher [plasma_current](#plasma_current) and reduced stability margins. The minimum safety factor $q_{\text{min}}$ and edge safety factor $q_{95}$ are key operational parameters. See [plasma_current](#plasma_current) and [magnetic_field](#magnetic_field) for field structure relationships.

Measurement methods:

Safety factor profiles are determined from equilibrium reconstruction using external magnetic measurements. The $q$-profile relates to [plasma_current_density](#plasma_current_density) through $\nabla \times \mathbf{B} = \mu_0 \mathbf{J}$ and can be inferred from [flux_loop_voltage](#flux_loop_voltage) measurements. MSE (motional Stark effect) diagnostics provide direct $q$-profile measurements in some devices.

Typical values:

On-axis: $q_0 = 0.7$-1.5, edge: $q_{95} = 3$-6 for stable operation. Operation below $q_{\text{min}} < 1$ leads to sawtooth oscillations. H-mode operation typically requires $q_{95} > 2.5$ for stability.

Sign convention: Positive when toroidal current and toroidal field are in same direction, following右手螺旋定则 for standard tokamak operation.

catalog_description: Toroidal component of magnetic field vector.
catalog_documentation:
Toroidal component of the [magnetic_field](#magnetic_field) vector $B_{\phi}$ in cylindrical coordinates. In tokamaks, the toroidal component is the dominant field component, produced by external toroidal field coils and providing plasma stability and particle confinement.

$$B_{\phi} = \mathbf{B} \cdot \hat{e}_{\phi}$$

where $\mathbf{B}$ is the total magnetic field in T and $\hat{e}_{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the toroidal direction.

Physical significance:

In tokamaks, the toroidal component is the dominant field component, produced by external toroidal field coils. Typical field strengths are 1-6 T on axis, with $B_{\phi} \gg B_R, B_Z$ for good magnetic confinement. The toroidal field provides plasma stability and determines the Larmor radius of particles. Field strength affects [safety_factor](#safety_factor) and MHD stability limits. See [poloidal_magnetic_field](#poloidal_magnetic_field) for field ratio and [magnetic_field](#magnetic_field) for total field structure.

Measurement methods:

Toroidal magnetic field is measured using magnetic probes and flux loops positioned around the plasma. [Flux_loop_voltage](#flux_loop_voltage) integration provides field change information. Equilibrium reconstruction codes determine internal field structure from external measurements. Toroidal field coils provide known field contribution for calibration. Field mapping requires multiple measurement locations around the torus.

Typical values:

On-axis: 2-6 T for medium to large tokamaks, decreasing as $B_{\phi} \propto 1/R$ for vacuum field. Field strength is primarily determined by external coil current and machine geometry.

Sign convention: Positive when anti-clockwise viewed from above, following standard tokamak conventions and consistent with [plasma_current](#plasma_current) direction for stable operation.

Toroidal component of the [magnetic_field](#magnetic_field) vector $B_{\phi}$ in cylindrical coordinates. In tokamaks, the toroidal component is the dominant field component, produced by external toroidal field coils and providing plasma stability and particle confinement.

$$B_{\phi} = \mathbf{B} \cdot \hat{e}_{\phi}$$

where $\mathbf{B}$ is the total magnetic field in T and $\hat{e}_{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the toroidal direction.

Physical significance:

In tokamaks, the toroidal component is the dominant field component, produced by external toroidal field coils. Typical field strengths are 1-6 T on axis, with $B_{\phi} \gg B_R, B_Z$ for good magnetic confinement. The toroidal field provides plasma stability and determines the Larmor radius of particles. Field strength affects [safety_factor](#safety_factor) and MHD stability limits. See [poloidal_magnetic_field](#poloidal_magnetic_field) for field ratio and [magnetic_field](#magnetic_field) for total field structure.

Measurement methods:

Toroidal magnetic field is measured using magnetic probes and flux loops positioned around the plasma. [Flux_loop_voltage](#flux_loop_voltage) integration provides field change information. Equilibrium reconstruction codes determine internal field structure from external measurements. Toroidal field coils provide known field contribution for calibration. Field mapping requires multiple measurement locations around the torus.

Typical values:

On-axis: 2-6 T for medium to large tokamaks, decreasing as $B_{\phi} \propto 1/R$ for vacuum field. Field strength is primarily determined by external coil current and machine geometry.

Sign convention: Positive when anti-clockwise viewed from above, following standard tokamak conventions and consistent with [plasma_current](#plasma_current) direction for stable operation.

catalog_description: Vertical component of magnetic field vector.
catalog_documentation:
Vertical component of the [magnetic_field](#magnetic_field) vector $B_Z$ in cylindrical coordinates. The vertical component is part of the poloidal magnetic field, essential for equilibrium force balance and plasma shaping in tokamak configurations.

$$B_Z = \mathbf{B} \cdot \hat{e}_Z$$

where $\mathbf{B}$ is the total magnetic field in T and $\hat{e}_Z$ is the unit vector in the vertical direction.

Physical significance:

The vertical component is part of the poloidal magnetic field, essential for equilibrium force balance and plasma shaping. Together with [radial_magnetic_field](#radial_magnetic_field), it forms the poloidal field that provides rotational transform of field lines. Vertical field strength affects plasma position control and [safety_factor](#safety_factor) profiles. See [poloidal_magnetic_field](#poloidal_magnetic_field) for vector relationships and [poloidal_magnetic_field](#poloidal_magnetic_field) for magnitude.

Measurement methods:

Vertical magnetic field is measured using magnetic probes and flux loops positioned above and below the plasma. [Flux_loop_voltage](#flux_loop_voltage) integration provides field change information. Equilibrium reconstruction codes invert external magnetic measurements to determine internal field structure. Vertical field analysis requires symmetric probe placement above and below the midplane. Field measurements are essential for plasma position control.

Typical values:

$|B_Z|$ ranges from milliTesla to 1 T, typically 1-2 orders of magnitude smaller than [toroidal_magnetic_field](#toroidal_magnetic_field). Vertical field strength varies with plasma position and external coil currents.

Sign convention: Positive upward (positive Z direction), following standard cylindrical coordinate conventions and consistent with tokamak geometry.
